title: Add up enough spinning circles and you can draw any closed outline, even a cat

cover.alt: Three line drawings on white, a sitting cat, a trotting horse and a triple spiral, each traced as one smooth closed curve.

body: A **Fourier series** can break any closed outline into circles: some spinning one way and some the other, at one, two, three or more turns per lap, each with its own size and starting angle. Stack them tip to tail and the tip of the last circle traces the shape. Big, slow circles give the rough form; small, fast ones add the detail, so the more you add, the closer the drawing gets. As Fourier analysis showed, any smooth closed curve can be matched as closely as you like this way, which is also why ancient astronomers’ circles riding on circles predicted the planets so well.

slides.alt: Animation of three outlines, a cat, a horse and a triple spiral, drawn with more and more Fourier terms. They start as rough blobs and triangles and sharpen into detailed shapes, then the sequence repeats.

slides.prompt: Ptolemy predicted the planets with circles riding on circles, called epicycles, and Earth at the centre. Why did it work so well?
slides.answer: Enough circles can fit any smooth path
slides.detail: As Fourier analysis later showed, enough epicycles can match any smooth curve to any accuracy. The model was flexible, not right: planets really move in near-ellipses around the Sun.

slides.question: In the clip, what makes the outlines sharper?
slides.explanation: Each extra term is another, faster circle that adds finer detail: the big slow ones set the rough shape, the small fast ones add ears, legs and curls.
